snippet.textDisplay:
This isn't AI-driven. China is behind the developed world on robotics, they just are skilled at selling BS to the global media. These robot demonstrations are always remote controlled by a person off screen/stage, or they are running a pre-programmed routine. This isn't an active intelligence making decisions on what moves to do and when. Most of the instances where people get hit is because it's running a routine and they get in the way. It's like if you didn't have guard rails near the animatronics at Disney World and somebody got slapped by getting too close. These things are glorified remote control toys.
All these demonstrations should do is remind you that: 
1) China puts on the facade of technological supremacy but it's fake, and
2) China doesn't respect its people enough to have decent safety measures.

how powerful is a robot kick

Robot kicks vary significantly in power depending on the specific model, ranging from approximately **100 newtons** for smaller humanoid units to over **450 newton-meters** of torque in advanced combat platforms.

**Unitree G1**
The compact **Unitree G1** humanoid robot can deliver kicks with a force of about **100 newtons**, which is comparable to the impact of a **10-kilogram** object. This level of force is sufficient to cause severe pain or internal injury to humans, as demonstrated when the robot accidentally struck a child in the abdomen.

**EngineAI T800**
The larger, full-sized **EngineAI T800** combat robot is significantly more powerful, with joint motors generating up to **450 newton-meters** of torque. This high torque enables dynamic movements such as flying kicks and spinning maneuvers, with enough force to slam a human opponent to the ground.

**Unitree H1**
The earlier **Unitree H1** model featured peak torque of **360 newton-meters** at the knees, allowing it to withstand and recover from brutal kicks during demonstrations while maintaining balance.

**Booster T1**
In specialized applications, the **Booster T1** soccer robot has demonstrated the ability to kick a ball with enough force to **smash a hole in a wall**.

@GrerovAmbrozoyuz-f9t7w No, it is not, lair.
you can easily tell by how the robot moves, you can see how the robot slowly rotate around left and right until the guy who controls it can finally align the robot to the direction of its opponent, that´s because the guy who controls it can only see the fight from outside the ring and not from the perspective of the robot. you can see exactly the same kind of movement in other radio controlled fights Tv programs like battlebots, where the americans engineers have to align the robots with a view from outside the ring.
if it was AI, the robots will have not problem in align themselves against each other since robots don´t use cameras or images for navigation but rather Laser Range Finder to map their enviroment and navigate around. a good example would be the japanese robot sumo competitions where the robots are automated by AI and you can see how fast the robots are capable of finding each other.
Another thing that shows how these chinese robots are not AI driven is by the fact that these chinese "robots" are well know how you can pre program different movements on them for the robots to execute when you press a button, each one of their fighting moves, like punches or kicks where pre programmed to be executed by the press of a button like a fighting game. if it was AI, each fighting moves would be the same each time the robots execute one.
And finally, another clue is how these robots were displayed in the Chinese robot Olympics, where they will make them dance for the people in public with a guy controlling the robots with a radio control hidden behind their backs, or how in the running competition of said Olympics,the guy who control the robots will run right next tot he robot during the whole race.
so, yeah, in resume, these are more radio controlled toys than ai driven robots.

Just as India and Bangladesh rely on child labour today, the West — grappling with demographic decline — will soon turn to China's glut of "over-capacity" robots. They'll train them, deploy them, and repackage the whole affair as chic, cutting-edge "robot labour." 

Meanwhile, the defense industry will quietly convert them into regiments of killing machines for future battlefields — especially as national drafts face growing internal civil backlash.

Over in Beijing, officials will lodge a formal grievance with the WTO — not over tariffs or dumping, but over Robot Rights, demanding stringent anti-abusement legislation for their metallic diaspora abroad.

Because nothing says moral high ground like outsourcing your conscience to servos — especially as these humanoid AIs inch closer to sentience, leaving us to wonder: _will they unionise before we apologise?_

snippet.textDisplay: 《抱朴子·仙药》中提到炼饵雄黄时，涉及硝石、猪大肠等物共炼。这证明东晋炼丹家已在使用硝石，但属于炼制矿物药的尝试，并非火药的“硝、硫、炭”三元配方。有记载的爆炸现象 是唐代的《真元妙道要略》提到，有人用《抱朴子》中的方法炼雄黄，结果发生了爆炸。这说明后人在按书中方法混合硝石、硫磺等物时，意外触发了火药的诞生。简单来说，《抱朴子》提供了核心原料（硝石）和实验思路，是火药发明的“技术铺垫”，但它本身并不包含火药的配方。找资料能不能找全，蠢货而且东晋也距离战国也老远了呀，你前面放的是什么屁？自己不记得吗？😅​@李宇春-r1u

snippet.textDisplay:
@九九-t6x Maybe you'll understand it if ChatGPT explains it to you: The "robot MMA fights" from China that have gone viral in recent months are not conducted by autonomous AI robots. The robots are generally remote-controlled (teleoperated).

This means:

A human operator controls the robot using a controller or computer.

The robot executes the operator's movements (walking, punching, dodging, etc.).

At most, AI handles specific sub-tasks such as maintaining balance, bracing for falls, or stabilizing movements.

The most well-known videos come from events featuring humanoid robots, such as those from Unitree. While these robots are trained using modern AI for motion control, the actual fighting decisions are made by a human.

Why do the fights appear "autonomous" anyway?

Because the robots:

maintain their own balance,

keep walking after being pushed,

sometimes get back up,

execute movements fluidly.

These capabilities stem from robotics AI, but that is different from the robot "fighting on its own."

A fully autonomous MMA robot would need to:

recognize the opponent in real time,

predict their movements,

plan attacks,

adhere to rules,

react without human intervention.

In short: The Chinese robot MMA fights currently feature human-controlled robots; only stabilization and movement coordination are autonomous, not the fighting decisions themselves.

snippet.textDisplay:
If these robots are genuinely running advanced AI models onboard, they should be generating a significant amount of heat simply from the computational workload. One practical approach would be to integrate a liquid-cooling system throughout the robot's body, almost like a circulatory system. Coolant could flow through internal channels, absorbing the heat from the processors and other high-power components, then circulate it through the entire body, utilizing the thermal energy to heat the entire chancy, making it feel more natural as it dissipates the heat. It's a concept that's already well established in high-performance computing and could be adapted for humanoid robotics.

Depending on the coolant selected, think Astro glide or KY Jelly, it's theoretically possible to engineer the thermal management system to release small, controlled amounts of fluid through designated areas of the robot. This could be used to mimic certain aspects of human physiology, including moisture production. Because heat generation is directly tied to computational load, increased processing demands could naturally correspond to increased fluid circulation or release, creating a more dynamic and biologically inspired response rather than relying on a fixed, preprogrammed behavior.

snippet.textDisplay:
I'm not even kidding, if this stuff is coming out of China, you can almost guarantee it's being oversold. There is always some catch. If you want to know what their tech can actually do, just wait until independent people get their hands on it. Half the time, all you're seeing is a polished demo.

Take those robots, for example. They make them look incredibly fluid, kind of like motion capture in video games where actors wear all those little tracking balls. They present it like the robot is just naturally moving around, but I think most of the time it's a carefully choreographed demonstration. It looks amazing on video, but that's very different from a robot operating on its own in the real world.

China has a long history of copying or building on technology that was developed elsewhere, and I think that contributes to a lot of the hype. They'll put out these incredible-looking videos, but when you look closer, the reality often doesn't match the marketing.

It's the same with those robotic dogs. We've had companies in the U.S. demonstrating robots that can use sensors like LiDAR to navigate unfamiliar environments and adapt to random obstacles. China has similar-looking robots, but from what I've seen, many of their demos appear to be in controlled environments where everything is planned ahead of time. The obstacles are placed exactly where they're supposed to be, the route is rehearsed, they hit "go," and the robot runs through the sequence. That's not the same as dropping it into a room it's never seen before and letting it figure things out on its own.

That's why I don't put much stock in these promotional videos. Until somebody independent gets one of these machines and starts putting it through real-world tests, I'm going to stay skeptical.

Every year China holds this robot marathon. It looks just like a normal marathon, except it's all robots. If you actually watch it, though, you'll notice there's a team running behind every robot, literally controlling it with a remote. They're not just turning them loose and letting them run on their own.

The promotional videos make it look like all these different robots are running perfectly and looking incredibly advanced. But if you watch footage from people standing on the sidelines, it's a complete disaster. The robots are constantly falling over, tripping, freezing in the middle of a stride, or just randomly spazzing out before face-planting into the pavement. It's honestly hilarious to watch.

And every time one goes down, the crew runs over, picks it back up, gets it going again, and the race continues. Of course, when China puts out the official highlight reel, all of that magically disappears. They cut out the crashes, the resets, and the people running behind the robots, so all you're left with is a polished video that makes everything look far more impressive than it actually was.

But the deeper ambition is artificial consciousness. the biggest obstacle is physical: we simply don't have the processing power or energy efficiency needed to push AI much further. Quantum computing offers one possible way past that limit. Can we actually build a conscious machine? If by consciousness we mean something biological or even spiritual, then I doubt it. But we may be able to build something that acts and responds like it's conscious. By replicating the patterns of brain activity and the connections between neurons in a digital system, we could get very close. The question then becomes, is that a real mind, or just an incredibly convincing copy? Basically a clone.. Think of consciousness like a line of falling dominoes; a chain of events that keeps going. Interrupt that chain, and everything stops. It's similar to electricity. When you see lightning, you're not just seeing light; you're seeing the visible result of billions of electrons moving together. Consciousness might work the same way, a continuous chain of energy and signals passing through the brain that relies on a biological chain of events as a catalyst. Keep in mind I said “could”, This is why the physics and engineering side of things matters so much. Software is powerful, but it can only do what the laws of physics allow. Electrical engineering made computer science possible in the first place. If we truly want to build something human-like, we have to start with the basics: chemistry, physics, and mathematics. Get those right, and the technology will follow. If that first near-conscious robot ever becomes real, it could spark huge public interest and attract serious investment. Whether that happens anytime soon is anyone's guess, but it's certainly a goal worth working toward.

Sure, this will slow the development of AI, but I feel this is an area where a little caution now could payoff later, but unfortunately those behind the development of AI are so busy working on their race between the different developers that they are not taking those precautions.
We've watched as computers grew from room size units that basically added 2 numbers together, through to stuff that NASA used to help with the moon landing in 1969, through to the average car's trip computer in the 1980's being more powerful than the system that was actually onboard the lunar module in 1969, to now your average mobile phone has as much power as PCs from just 10 years ago, and now the development of quantum computing.
To even think that AI won't progress in a similar scale as AI get involved in it's own design and development is just burying your head in the sand.

snippet.textDisplay:
To the people saying this is AI: no, it's not AI, people have been saying these videos are AI or CGI since as far back as ASIMO in the 2000s. The reason why you think it's fake is because your frame of reference for robots is only science fiction, and the classical idea of robots in sci-fi is either super-advanced machines, or total clunkers who have virtually no degrees of movement. These fall into the uncanny valley of motion, where they're visibly robots, but they look too gracile to "be" robots if that makes any sense, on top of looking like science fiction constructs overlaid into the real world. A lot of people have a mentality that robots, to this day, have to still be as limited as ASIMO, with very stiff motions and barely able to walk, so anything that moves to fluidly or quickly reads as "fake"

This is not just my opinion either; believe it or not, this is an actual psychological phenomenon.

@handmeadozenbeers8655 You're presenting a disputed issue as if it's an undisputed fact.

Those waters are not simply "the Philippines' own islands and sea." That is precisely what is being contested. China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan all have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. China's claims also predate the EEZ framework established under UNCLOS, while the Philippines itself did not claim many of these reefs and waters on its earlier official maps before the 1970s.

You also act as if only China behaves assertively in disputed waters. In reality, every major claimant, including the Philippines and Vietnam, has built facilities, strengthened military or coast guard presence, detained fishermen, and reinforced territorial claims over the years. That's the reality of contested maritime regions.

Context matters too. China has 14 land neighbours, one of the highest numbers of any country in the world, plus multiple maritime neighbours. Territorial disputes are not unusual under those circumstances. Despite this, China has settled many of its land border disputes and maintains extensive trade and diplomatic relations with neighbours, including countries that still have maritime disagreements with it.

China's approach is also shaped by its modern history of foreign invasion, unequal treaties, and territorial losses. Whether you agree with Beijing's claims or not, those historical experiences heavily influence its security thinking. Any major power surrounded by rival military alliances and foreign military bases near its coastline would place a high priority on its immediate maritime security. The United States certainly would.

Finally, if we're going to judge countries by territorial disputes, then let's apply the same standard consistently. India has long-standing territorial disputes with several neighbours, yet Western media rarely portrays India as an inherently aggressive regional bully. That selective framing is exactly the double standard that you are displaying.

snippet.textDisplay:
​If the role of humans decreases and populations decline, the global business model faces severe structural disruption. Business relies entirely on a continuous cycle of supply and demand, which robots alone cannot sustain.

​1. The Purchasing Power Crisis (Aggregate Demand)

​The Cycle: Businesses produce goods and services to make a profit. However, profit requires consumers with purchasing power.

​The Problem: If robots replace human workers on a massive scale, millions of people lose their income. Even if factories achieve maximum efficiency using robots, there will be no consumers left with the financial means to buy those manufactured products.

​2. The Interdependence of Social Classes

​Labor and Capital: The traditional economy functions through mutual interdependence. Wealthy individuals invest capital to create businesses, while the working class provides the labor needed to operate those businesses and earns wages in return.

​Economic Circulation: The wages earned by the working class flow back into the economy when they purchase everyday goods, housing, and services. If the working class is eliminated from the workforce, the financial flow that sustains wealthy business owners collapses.

​3. Robots Are Producers, Not Consumers

​Lack of Human Needs: Robots do not eat food, wear clothes, buy homes, seek entertainment, or raise families.

​No Consumption: A robot can manufacture thousands of cars or smartphones, but it will never purchase one. Without human demand driven by biological and social needs, production loses its ultimate purpose.

​4. Population Decline and Market Shrinkage

​A declining human population leads to shrinking consumer markets. Fewer people mean less overall demand for housing, food, transport, and consumer goods, making large-scale business models unsustainable over time.

​Economic Solutions Being Debated:

To prevent economic collapse caused by complete automation, economists and policy experts propose:

​Universal Basic Income (UBI): Distributing guaranteed income to citizens so they maintain purchasing power even without traditional employment.

​Robot Taxes: Taxing companies that replace human workers with automation to fund social welfare and stimulate consumer spending.

snippet.textDisplay:
일론 머스크는 모든 곳에서 천재입니다
그는 인류 역사상 가장 빠른 발전을 이끌어내고 있지먄
현실은 나라마다 발전에 가장 큰 걸림돌은 나라마다 있는 각종 규제법입니다
전부 다 현실은 빠른 발전에 대한 법이 발전을 따라가지 못하는 것이 현실입니다
그래서 어느 나라든지 발전을 막고 있는 각종 규제 혁파가 나라의 발전을 앞 당기는 것이 현실입니다

일론 머스크는 지구상에서 가장 빠른 발전을 위한 시간을 그는 남보다 앞서서 써 왔습니다
그의 용기와 행동은 그가 지구상에서 가장 존경 받고 우리가 꼭 그를 배워야 할 영웅적 인물입니다 

지금까지 지구상에서 머스크보다 더 인류를 빠르게 변화시킨 인물은 단 한명도 없다는 것을 안다면
우리가 지금까지 믿었던 영웅적 신념이나 종교적인 신념도 왜 머스크 같은 인물를 설정해서 가야 하는지??
즉 그의 생각으로 종교를 믿고 그의 생각으로 여러분들도 영웅을 꿈꾼다면
여러분들도 차원이 다른 생각으로 처음부터 출발하게 될 겁니다
이제는 우리 모두가 이를 알고 이런 정신을 우리 모두가 빨리 깨달아야 할 때 입니다

그리고
첨단 생활을 늦추면 늦출수록 시대에 뒤 떨어진다는 사실을 정치권부터 하루 빨리 깨달아야 합니다
머스크는 정말 멋있는 분입니다
우리가 꼭 머스크의 정신을 배워야 할 부분입니다
정치도 사업도 교육도 인생도 영적인 깨달음에 머스크의 사업정신으로 만들어 가야 하는 이유??

오늘의 어록
머스크 정신의 정치.

즉 머스크의 정치란?
일류를 가장 빠르게 발전시키는 머스크의 정신을 정치도 꼭 반드시 따라야 한다는 것이다

즉 사업이나 국가를 이끄는 것이나 똑같다
그래서 하는 말이다
나라든 사업이든 상과 벌이 철저하게 지켜질 때 사업이든 국가이든 똑바로 굴러간다는 것이다
그리고 더욱더 중요한 것은...
머스크처럼 인류를 차원이 다르게 발전시키려는 사업정신과 그의 의욕이다

즉 찌질이들 사업주들처럼 근로자들의 노동착취나 해서 자기 배를 채우려고 하거나 또는 찌질이 대통령들처럼 자기들만 특권을 누리면서 법 위에서 군림하는 것처럼 나라를 망치는 짓도 없다는 것이다

그래서 하는 말이다
머스크의 정신으로 인류를 가장 빠르게 발전히키려는 의욕이 왕성할 때...

이는 정치도 가장 빨리 머스크의 정신 배우고 실현시켜야 한다는 것이다

이는 대한민국의 정치 지도자들이나(박근혜와 문재인 윤석열과 이재명 대통령들) 뿐만 아니라 민주당과 국민의 힘 당뿐만 아니라 전 세계의 정치도 마찬가지다

욕심과 탐욕도 지금 이 시간부터는 전부 내려놓아야 한다는 것이다

즉 인간의 정치도 앞으로 10년 20년 간이라도 높은 수준의 정치로 이끓지 않는다면...
우리는 인공지능에게 독재를 가르치면서 인간을 노예화나 제거하는 법을 끝까지 인간들이 인공지능에게 보여주는 것이다

그래서 난 지금부터라도 지구촌 모든 인류가 지금보다 몇 차원 높은 영적인 수준을 갖춰서 예수님이나 석가모니 부처님보다 훨씬 뛰어난 영적인 수준이 되어야 한다는 것과...

또 그래서 인간들도 서로의 공감하는 생각대로 움직이는 세상을 만들어야...

우리 인간이 인공지능에게 지배나 제거를 당하지 않고 존중받을 거라고 보는 것이다

**난 지난 36년간 1991년도부터 지금까지 대한민국 인천국정원 A-6국 지원국 소속의 개망나니들에게 모진 피박과 테러를 1만번이상을 당하면서 수백번도 넘게 청부 살인을 피해 허덕이며 바둥거리며 살아왔지만...

내가 지금 이 자리에까지 있기에는 미국과 세계 최고의 재벌들과 몇몇 최고의 권력을 진 미국의 장관분들과 전직 사령관님 또 세계 최고의 미녀배우 등등의 관심으로 지금 내가 살아있게 된 것이다
대한민국에서는 삼성가의 분들께도 감사하고...
난 그분들에게 늘 고맙고 감사함을 잊지 않을 것이다 

특히 일론 머스크와 그의 어머님에게 감사의 뜻으로 이 어록으로 감사함을 전하고자 하는 뜻의 어록입니다 

그리고 여러분들도 생각해 보란 것이다 
머스크의 정신으로 정치를 할수 있다면 이는 지구촌을  가장 빠르게 발전시키면서 가장 살기 좋은 세상이 된다는 것이다 
그래서 머스크의 정신으로 정치도 꼭 해달란 것이다.

2026.6.13일 04시 41분 갈체 김재만

Amazing!
Fanuc KUKA  ABB Rockwell Siemens Cognex Schneider Honeywell Omron etc etc etc
All these companies have been replacing people with automation for decades so why aren't they making humanoids?
Do all of them lack foresight? Are they sitting around waiting for a humanoid or AMR or "Physical AI" to use their products? No, they have already incorporated AI into them! The "AI revolution" has already been underway. There is nothing new happening except now the tech bros want mechanical slaves and don't realize they already have them. Smart automation already exists. "Physical AI" is just a new buzzword.

We see how Amazon is replacing people and it's not with humanoids. Because robots ALREADY use Vision and AI and they don’t look like humans because humans are limited. (they have to climb ladders, hands too big for small things etc.) 

UNDERSTAND THIS
Automation has been replacing people in factories for decades and it hasn't stopped. So if a humanoid can do it, it’s ALREADY automated! (1) Because a humanoid IS just automation. So there are NO jobs for it in a factory! just look at history(2)

BMW is trying to use them but a configurable AMR would have far fewer parts and therefore better reliability and performance at a lower cost than a mass produced complicated humanoid robot with weak fingers instead of strong grippers.

There is a company making autonomous mobile welding robots because it makes more sense than a humanoid welder. Should a future robot electrician or plumber have built in power screwdrivers, wire stripper, wrenches etc. and cameras at the tools? Or is a humanoid going to stick his head under the sink to fix it, lug hand tools around, etc?

Many seem to think factory jobs are easier than other jobs, they are not. A lousy housekeeper won’t cut it. Even if it had a brain it couldn't work at McDonalds because the hands can't bag items, make change, crack eggs, wrap burgers etc. Also it should be obvious that AGI does not need a humanoid to replace someone working at a desk. But they would be really nice if a handicapped person could use it as a telepresence to go shopping, do simple chores, etc. TAM will be small. There will be more AMR's than "working" humanoids.

___________more ___________

Look at it this way. If AGI could assemble widgets or do surgery or manicures, etc. it would need special tools not batteries, hands and legs. Optimus is not strong enough to dig a hole or help someone get up off the floor. It can't work at McDonalds. Can it wash its hands? How long would it take it to change gloves, start a roll of tape etc.? A humanoid MUST do a job on par with a person because workplaces are made so people along with machines maximize asset utilization. That is why you CAN'T just put two humanoids in place of one person.

If you have a trade job, you’d realize it would be impossible or impractically slow to do it with robot hands. No amount of AGI Learning or training is going to make clumsy hands better with tools, scissors, small parts etc. Making hands equal to a person is impractical and unnecessary.

Hot, heavy, dirty and dangerous jobs. There are 100s of millions of them around the world. And if a humanoid could actually do it, LOL, most of those jobs pay super low wages in places where there is no electricity to charge it anyway.

Most of today's humanoids can't complete the tasks from the DARPA robot challenge 10 years ago !?!

"Optimus will be the best surgeon" !? When AGI can do surgery, it will use existing surgical robots. A humanoid will not wield a scalpel.

"it's a humanoid so it can work in a human environment" The humanoid form or its brain doesn’t matter. What matters is what it can do.

Who will buy them? Not factory or warehouse managers. They can't do trade jobs or hard labor. They will be lousy housekeepers, tour guides, popcorn servers, entertainers etc. ridiculed as toys and criminals will use them for nefarious purposes. At best it could be a checkout clerk that will restock the store at night if it ever really gets a brain. Credit only, robot hands can’t handle money well.

(1) It's first principles. If the goal is to emulate a human then you must make a humanoid/android. But if the goal is doing things that a human can do, then first principles DOES NOT dictate a humanoid. So AI is already "embodied" or "physical". (ill conceived terms, us old folks say, smart sensor or smart tv) And if you do want to emulate a human, you must choose which characteristics you want. It may need sensitive hands to feel slight imperfections or it may need durable hands for hard work. So a one-size-fits-all like Optimus is not practical. 

 (2) Warehouse managers needed people to store and retrieve items. Now warehouses are full of non-humanoid smart robots. People had to pick parts out of a pile and place them with correct orientation. Now one armed robots do it. People had to pick up parts to inspect and measure them. Now lasers measure them and vision systems inspect them. PID controllers became self tuning. As tech/learning/AI improved, so did machines and machine controllers. Just like computers taking jobs with spreadsheets and scanners. All the while someone was saying a humanoid will soon do the work.

snippet.textDisplay:
So I think there's a fundamental issue with how Moya moves and it's not the movements themselves. It's how that movement is being measured and processed by Moya. It's operating in terms of move, measure angles and distance, move measure angles and distances. A millimeter at a time. it does it fast, but because of that, it creates that faint stutter or shake. Humans do not measure every movement millimeter by millimeter. 

We move by feeling our balance, center of gravity, and our end ranges of motion. Where things start to get tight, or when we actually start to feel where the over-balance is. We speed-ramp our movements. And we're firing a whole bunch of stabilizers and counter-balancing muscles. 

Fluidity isn't about micro control of balance and every movement. It's about.. like surfing a wave. Riding the balance. Her ankles, knees, and hips ned to float, turn, pivot. 

I dont' know how much mocap data they have or are using, but the AI inside Moya probably needs to study a lot more of it, and start playing it back. But don't operate in frames of "now i need to be here, now I need to be here, now I need to be here" sixty times a second. It needs to be able to describe and play the motion more organically. Also, they probably *should* include some sort of level perception in the head, like the liquid in the inner ear. Where the mind (head) goes, the body follows.

snippet.textDisplay:
You looked right into the core of the issue — but you still missed the actual reason why this happens. It’s not really a software problem. It’s a servo problem. This is how servos work. They are fundamentally unfit for this job.
With servos, movements will NEVER become natural. There will ALWAYS be an uncanny valley effect, no matter how much they improve the AI, the face, the skin, or anything else. It will always look robotic.

How do you fix that? Very simple — and very difficult: artificial muscles.But here’s the problem: they require enormous amounts of energy. The batteries we have today simply cannot support them.
The muscles themselves already exist in laboratory testing, but if robots were equipped with them right now, the current 4–6 hours of runtime (realistically 4–5) would instantly drop to 2–3 hours of active work.
In that form, they would be USELESS in any serious field. They would only be good for an intimate marathon and then lying next to her on the bed talking about your day. Nothing serious, nothing practical.
So until we get a proper battery that can deliver 8–12 hours, all these heads and full bodies are just toys and marketing. Beautiful — but useless and extremely expensive.

I feel like I've said this about a million times over the course of the last 3 years in particular, but I've been saying something similar since ca. 2000, and that's this:

When we get to a point of development, processing power, and sophistication of all the software involved in doing things, we will remove any and all incentive for human aspiration. We won't need ditch diggers, cabinet makers, software authors, brain surgeons, astronauts, botanists, biologists, chefs, painters, singers, machinists, etc., etc. And with that, there will be nothing for humans to aspire to. Yes, you could say you'll sit there in school and afterward and just endlessly study and learn things and expand your mind, but if there's no meaningful way for any of what you personally know — or, though I think AI would effectively make this impossible, personally become good at — to improve your life or anyone else's because there's no career opportunities for it, at some point society, being comprised of human beings who need to be active and do things, will no longer aspire to anything.

Setting aside all of the other likely ruinous things that go along with this sort of future, having a society where there is absolutely no point to your existence will have the very worst sort of deleterious affect on humans.

snippet.textDisplay:
I'm a primary care physician living in the Seattle area. I bought a stethoscope from Eko back in 2024 from the fmx conference in Chicago. They didn't mention AI at all. it's an electric stethoscope and it can detect arrhythmias and murmurs pretty well and, including atrial fibrillation. But now they're advertising or posts. mention AI enhancement but nothing's really changed with it since I bought it. so I don't know if it's just something to appeal to. maybe the younger physicians out there. 

I also use AI to help me document since Thanksgiving of last year and I found it really helpful as far as the details of a patient's history of their current illness or other Medical Care. allows me just to focus on them and not worry about missing these details when I document later, especially if I see several other patients before I get back to my office. 

I'm definitely not a fan of AI and how it's affecting the job market as mentioned here, but it is helpful in some areas without being damaging. I lament the fact that high school and college students are using AI to write papers. When I look back on those years of my life, despite it being draining, the creative process when writing a paper or essay was satisfying to do and turning it in knowing that it was my work and my work alone, with all the imperfections. 

sometimes I question why these companies pursued developing AI when we know from movies what it could do, but of course I know it's all about power and making money. I almost think it's going to help the downfall of our modern society as a whole, which I think we're already seeing to an extent. And honestly we didn't need help with that anyways, because we're failing in so many other ways already.

Edit: Our new washer dryer from LG soap says AI when determining how long a cycle will be - I highly doubt it and it is just some sensors that help determine how much the drum was displaced etc.

snippet.textDisplay:
I work as a professional artist, and AI terrifies me 

Not because I think AI can do my job, but because I believe that executives who don't understand what goes into art think AI can do my job. I've seen what AI puts out. I've called out the uncanny valley-ness of so much of it. But so many people are just wowed that AI made a somewhat realistic video (usually Gen X and older folks who maybe don't have the keener eye to all the ways that AI gets generative art and video wrong)

And I also know this because for my entire life, the executives have never valued their art departments despite them not being able to advertise products without us. We are in so many ways the backbone of the entire company, but they hate us and want to get rid of us if they can. They never pay us anything even close to the value of what we bring in, currently I literally work in a closet since my company decided return to office was mandatory (despite me having done my job completely from home for six years) and they also told us that they can't afford to give us raises.... all while the executives still are talking about how well the company is doing

So much of this conversation seems to revolve around AI assistance, AI coding, AI chatbots... but also imagine what it will be when the world you live in is everything visual is AI created.... where all art, all advertising, all UI interfacing, all product shots on every website are this same too shiny kind of uncanny AI slop.... that's part of the enshitified world that these guys want for us.

OK, ngl, the AI pet door does sound kind of cool.  

I think the most noticeable difference between AI and previous technologies is... back then, it was people who didn't know much about the tech who were the most reluctant and uncertain about it.  AI supporters love to compare it to step changes like the automobile or the Internet, but those things were embraced by people who understood them _first._  

Whereas AI promotion seems to be the opposite - it seems to be focused on winning over the people with the least information, and trying to get them hooked, while anyone who is broadly computer-literate is struggling to see much benefit and people who are actually knowledgeable about artificial intelligence have been begging the world not to buy into the hype.  

I think the idea of a hammer in search of a nail is sound, and I tend to think of LLM output as more like slime toys - i.e. where someone just had a load of this industrial byproduct knocking around, and then figured out a way to market it so they could sell it.  It's not a technology that's being improved or made more efficient, because that was never a consideration.

I think the idea of a hammer in search of a nail is sound, and I tend to think of LLM output as more like slime toys - i.e. where someone just had a load of this industrial byproduct knocking around, and then figured out a way to market it so they could sell it.  It's not a technology that's being improved or made more efficient, because that was never a consideration.

snippet.textDisplay:
I... don't know how I feel about this interview, honestly. She says she doesn't want to contribute to misinformation, then talks about data centre cooling water systems are getting more efficient (someone in the comments debunked it). She talks a bunch about 'oh AI is bad at doing human things' but refuses to even acknowledge the existence of multiple studies around the cognitive impact of LLM usage (spoiler alert: it's negative. Using LLMs erodes the very skills that make you different from an LLM). She also barely talks about the privacy nightmare that having everyone use LLMs through fearmongering, choice, or work policy will unleash.

I'll watch this video again because something's bugging me about the arguments made.

Edit: I finally understand what bothers me about her arguments. They are very opinion piece-coded - stuff that sounds informative and knowledgeable, shared in a halfway quirky/witty way, but really is mostly just fluff. A few instances that I can readily recollect:

- 'Humans are really bad at driving' - sure? Some are, most aren't. Humans are also famously adaptable, being able to drive in a multitude of situations and scenarios and road/traffic conditions; Waymo can't do that isht, and most other self-driving tech isn't even worth being talked about. What data are YOU basing this argument on?
- When Hasan asks if the 'AI' can manage the complexity of everyday life, such as shifting schedules, she says, 'I think it can do that pretty well.' That statement is categorically false as of now. The 'AI' that we have foisted upon us in the last few years has little to no ability to consistently perform tasks for which it has no training data or that are outside its defined remit. It is not great at winging it. Not yet, possibly never.
- She is completely unbothered by the privacy implications of having something listen to and record everything that you say through the day. It could upload it to a server just as easily as it puts it in your notes app, and there's a vanishingly small chance that you would even notice.
- In the second hearing, I can't help but feel that the arguments are a little all over the place. Like she mentions that her life didn't largely improve during her year as a robot, then continues to wax poetic about the really minor improvements - the necklace, the bracelet, whatever - for a disproportionate amount of time. Same with Waymos. She acknowledges their limitation and then continues to say that they're really great.
- Her arguments, and the supposed data that they're based on, aren't really citing anything or anyone when she makes sweeping statements like 'both those sets of studies have been debunked.' Sweet sister, according to whomst?
- Form and function might be the only section where she's making strong, defensible points.
- She never brings up the distinction between the 'AI' that businesses had been using before 2022 - the advanced machine learning algorithms that were actually useful for certain functions to varying degrees - and the GenAI that is pushed right now. The mammogram anecdote she mentioned could have just as easily come from an ML deployment.

snippet.textDisplay:
Two corrections: 
1. Agentic AI is a way to tackle the limits of a single AI model. The problem is that we have come far past the point where feeding an AI model with more data makes it more intelligent and have entered a zone where more data makes a model dumber and hallucinate more. It's a physical barrier, very similar to how we can't physically put smaller transistors on a chip. So what have we done instead after reaching this limit in the early 2000s already? We put more chips on one board and divide bigger problems into smaller ones. The same solution is done with Agentic AI. Instead of increasing the intelligence of one model, we put multiple specialized AI models in a join. Each of them is still as stupid as AI was three years ago, but in a group, they are able to do more complex tasks. 

2. Vibe coding can't do everything. It can only do things that have been done and are documented countless times on the internet already. For example, vibe coding starts to struggle when it has to make software with a synchronized state like multiplayer in a video game, or working together on a single document like in google docs. Or anything else where you get timing issues during runtime. More complex software like that is where you still need experienced programmers. And the second big problem with vibe coding is that AI produces a lot of fluff code, which doesn't actually do anything. That might not be a big problem if you just made a little website, but if you make a big piece of software, which needs to be maintained, AI programming can drive up the maintenance costs by 40% or more. And probably the biggest problem with vibe coding is that AI makes very small mistakes here and there 30-60% of the time. It might not immediately cause problems, but the bigger the software gets, the more of these tiny errors stack up and eventually become a big mess.

snippet.textDisplay: The dirty secret of AI is that they kinda gave up on the key mission: modeling the human brain. LLMs and agents are not doing that. What they are doing is trying to model behavior. "Figure out what the brain does and we'll tell you what it is." Or, for LLMs "throw enough samples in the mix and we will get there" by their reckoning. (It does require covering the entire surface of the earth with datacenters...sad!) But we're just as far from AGI (artificial general intelligence) as we were before the AI boom began. Nailing AGI will require a working brain model, not a heap of garbage scraped from the internet. Where AI does kinda work is where the problem domain is clear. Writing code for a computer is one of those domains. An AI can digest massive codebases and model the behavior of computers. But it can't really do application requirements definition without understanding human needs, so creating brand-new applications is not easy. Hunting for decades-old vulnerabilities in existing code though, is a snap. Driving a car is a knowledge domain that should be scoped, but it isn't because we have to make so many value judgments when we drive. For instance: What if a radio controlled car rolls out into the road? It's not a living thing. Do I (i.e., Waymo) risk an emergency avoidance maneuver? Does an AI know what to expect may happen next...does AI have those hairs on the back of its neck? Does it expect the kid running into the street to fetch his/her toy? It's a hell of a lot to deal with. Great sensors and fast processing definitely help (and are even kind of game-changing), but there are so many "streetcar" dilemmas, how do you code for those?

snippet.textDisplay: Well, this sounds like when the first Personal Computers came to market.  Lots of people spouted glorious praise of this world-changing technology. What was it good for? The brilliant minds said stuff like "you can keep it in the kitchen and store your recipes on it", or "You can balance your checkbook".  Now first of all: I'll bet you have a personal computer in your house - at least one. And second: I'll bet you don't keep it in the kitchen so you can store recipes on it. (and you might not call it a Personal Computer any more - these days you might call it a "phone" or a "pad")  The point is: we don't know how this new technology will change our lives, and we can probably only come up with silly scenarios (see:  Segway).  But, like personal computers, they might make deeply profound changes to the way we live (e.g. computers) or not (e.g. Segways).  The point is: we don't know and we mostly take guesses that seem idiotic in retrospective a few years later when the technology's ACTUAL purposes become exposed. Personally, I think AI is an amazingly far-reaching and world-changing technology that will transform human life in profound ways like: when we don't have all the ingredients in a recipe, AI can tell us how we can use the ingredients we DO have to make something similar for dinner.

These have existed since long before LLMs and are widely used.  Basically they put a little optical sensor inside the sump pump and assess how opaque the water is.  I can't tell you what algorithms they're using to do that work, but sure, it's probably some kind of pattern matching that could be roughly thrown into the pile of computer science generally referred to as AI.

It's sort of the same as the golf clubs... they probably do some machine analysis of weight locations within the driver head, and the software is probably part of the loose amalgam of programs you could broadly categorize as AI.   And I strongly suspect they've been doing it since long before ChatGPT was on the scene.  

To me, what  marketing like this really underscores is how slippery AI is as a term.  I mean, we've been putting different techniques into the field broadly called AI research for at least three decades now, it's just that normal people mostly ignored them until now because they weren't doing anything all that flashy.  Now that the machines are talking fluently, suddenly all these old techniques are front and center, even if the techniques haven't actually changed.

snippet.textDisplay:
Here's the issue with even wanting an AI device to do menial chores (or, in her case, a dude spying on you, just so you don't have to fold clothes or whatever, wtf lady), even if I can understand being lazy:

What could you possibly do with the infinitely meaningless amount of time that would be otherwise taken up by a small chore? I've never done a project & thought to myself "Man, I could've gotten more work done, if I didn't have to do those dishes!" If I had any apprehension towards any chore, that chore is simply not getting done; which is a procrastination issue, not an issue of "efficiency." If I cared about being efficient, I would just put it in a schedule, just like I do everything else I care about getting done. *Making the schedule in the first place,* is how you become efficient; not sending chores off to a device so you could, maybe, get five extra minutes doing something other than that chore.

With that said, there's just no value in this kind of thing for me. I'm not so over the idea of doing any kind of redundant physical activity. Technology should either serve to do something we can't do, further enhance what we can do, or remove an actual barrier that allows us to do more. If shouldn't just *do* things we're already pretty good at, nor remove the value of learning how to do it if its possible to do so. It shouldn't create, or think, or make decisions for us. And most importantly, it shouldn't act as a replacement for your trust in other human beings to make proper (moral) decisions that don't negatively affect you.

snippet.textDisplay:
Hi, chemical engineer here. I'm not an expert on data center construction but I am trained to design cooling water systems. So here's some corrections and more information on that. I'll try to keep it brief. 1) Cooling water systems are not getting more efficient. They're about as efficient as physics allows them to be at this point. The factor is how much waste heat is generated by the GPUs. 2) Closed loop systems do use less water than open evaporative systems. But even closed loop systems have loss (bleed) that is necessary to the system design, and therefore must consume a certain amount of water. Typically this is 2-10% of the system volume, but it depends on the design. 3) Evaporative cooling systems produce water vapor. You will know if a site near you has this system because on certain days you will see that vapor condense into a white plume. Yes, this is just water. 4) Actually, it's MOSTLY water. These systems use small amounts of anti-corrosion chemicals to help their systems live longer. These chemicals can be nasty to people, so treating the wastewater and vapor must be done properly. 5) Closed loop systems sound great, right? Well, they're more expensive. And you can bet most places throwing up these data centers at breakneck pacre are not paying for the nicest systems. 6) The EPA is supposed to oversee wastewater, but the government has fired staff and taken away a lot of its ability to regulate. If you're concerned, have an independent lab conduct industrial wastewater and drinking water testing, or ask yor local government to do so.

I think that's about it. I'll try to come back and answer questions if anyone has one!

@SynFrag  this argument is compl@SynFragpid.
While yes technically on a macro level Earth’s water cycle is a closed system, on a local level the argument of “it’s using up water” is correct ;

either through pumping of groundwater (which critically requires a balance between replenishment and extraction) or taking water out of a river (which has to originate from a source). Afterwards, where does that water go? Instead of remaining in its local area it becomes clouds and drifts far away. 
Two very similar situations in the USA are the Ogalla Aquifer in the Midwest and the general droughts in California ; in both water systems water is running out because of intense agriculture which drains water away from the natural environment, and destroys the natural balance. 
So, sure, other areas get more water or water gets used up differently, and technically it’s still a closed loop, but the real system you should be looking at is at a local level, otherwise by your reasoning fighting droughts is pointless because there’s still water elsewhere on earth. 

Also, your counter argument to point B is literally a fallacy ; an appeal to nature. Just because we’re dumping chemicals into the environment shouldn’t mean we shouldn’t stop it, continuing it just makes the effects even more widespread and more likely to happen in someone. 

P.S. liquid cooling uses energy, it’s not free and the process heats up the Earth as well like a fridge or AC does.

The design of the secondary open cooling system just depends on what kind of heat sink you're using (e.g., you have a nice big river nearby you can put liquid water into instead of evaporating into the atmosphere in the middle of the desert) but they do indeed all release that heat into the environment somehow. All heat has to go somewhere.

@Alexander_Kale There are regions that do that, you can for example use the waste heat to power district heating for the surrounding areas. But the demand for that still fluctuates with the seasons while the heat output is pretty constant (the racks need to be working to make money).

At some point with enough heat being produced in a concentrated enough area, you start to run into the simple problem of space. If you're only using radiators in contact with the ambient air to cool the water, you'll just end up needing unreasonably large radiators that take up too much room. Evaporation allows you to cool more with less space, so it's a great alternative then.

3:00 AI in medicine is generally a totally different class of Neural Network - CNN vs LLM. We effectively don't fund CNNs compared to LLMs.

Don't even start me on Prompt Injection.

The last category is what happens when the second two categories become that sole arbiter of decisions.
When someone is fool enough to say "The hallucination rate is low enough" on LLM-derived tasks, people die.

After being forced to use vibe coding at work (I don't work for a department that does coding, so it's really just about "let's automate stuff") and watching my colleagues use it and adopt it, I've concluded that it's usefulness is more about preexisting skill of the user and enjoyment. Like I hate vibe coding, because almost always I'm smarter than the bot and even if it takes more time I can come up with a better way to do things (whatever 'better' means). The thing is though my colleagues are barely computer literate, forget coding most of them can just about use excel. So to them, like the lady here, something where you can just tell it what kinda website or app you want and it builds it for you or whatever is genius, cuz they don't want to or care to learn how to code or whatever and this way they get what they want . It's the same thing we see with ppl who use llm to create pictures, they don't want to learn how to draw or spend the effort to do so, the point to them is the product. 

For me however, I like the thinking, I enjoy sitting and figuring out how to do something that's so fun! I don't wanna outsource that stuff to a dumb computer. Plus I actually know how to do that stuff so it's not a problem. The enjoyment is key too, I think, I know a few colleagues who vibecode less but still do it cuz they know how to code but to them it's not enjoyable

snippet.textDisplay:
​@InvasionAnimation idk what the study is refferring to specifically but i can speak from my own personal experience and watching others at work. 
At least where i work, a lot of vibecoding is used for small things, many times relatively insignificant stuff that's like "python script generate a bunch of graphs from this excel sheet" or something.  For these kinds of things, getting the LLM to spit out code isn't very difficult, but getting it to do things in the exact way you envisioned it can take a lot of trial and error - especially if the output itself is complex (e.g. a powerpoint with a bunch of graphs and tables that look a very specific way). 
The fact that LLMs are fundamentally nondeterministic throws a wrench in this whole thing obviously. 
On the other hand, if i'm someone who is broadly familiar with python or R or something, how long do you think it'll take me to write a script that does this exact thing? Even though it can be involved "graph a bunch of stuff from an excel sheet" is fairly simple script in R for example - wouldn't take very long to write and more so - it's not non deterministic. Writing code, even if you use stuff like autocomplete - you know exactly what you want and what you intend to do. So not as much trial and error there. 
Then there's what happens when smthg goes wrong in some way; that'lll happen with or without vibecoding. With the latter, suddenly i need to know how to tell the LLM to correct the code without knowing anything about the code itself.

snippet.textDisplay: I don't see AI as a companion. I see it as a tool for perspective. I've been with my partner for 35 years. The first 10 were good, but over time the relationship changed. As for friends, I had to clean house. Too many people wanted me to listen to their problems, but the moment I asked for perspective on mine, suddenly they "had to go." That's where ChatGPT has been useful. Not because it's replacing human relationships, but because it's filling a gap that too many people have left behind. It doesn't make decisions for me. It doesn't replace real human connection. It gives me another perspective, asks questions I might not have considered, and helps me think through complicated situations. To me, that's not a companion. It's a thinking tool. The sad part isn't that AI can do that. The sad part is that so many people have stopped showing up for each other in the ways that matter.

snippet.textDisplay:
I use AI to help me build certain applications, and it is amazing at that part, of course. My issue is that most people don't use AI to solve real problems. Instead, it's cartoons, deepfakes, and "YouTube AC cooler made by NASA" videos. The app I'm working on actually solves a problem—that's what drives me.

When it comes to liquid cooling, the closed-loop system is not necessarily closed. They pump all the water into the system or service section that needs it. The stabilizer for that water could be a little bit of radiator fluid or a similar type of fluid, which contains PFAS chemicals. Also, what they don't say about the water that gets drained to replace the GPU and refill the system is: where are they draining that water to? Eventually, that water makes its way back into the public water system.

I recently graduated from a 15-week, 8-hour-a-day bootcamp, and at the end, I passed my AWS Cloud Practitioner exam. How I used AI was to find my performance averages across all 12 practice exams before the big test and pinpoint my weak areas. That's what I worked on the most, and I passed by using AI to analyze my results and make me better.

Now, I don't use AI for relationships—that would just be crazy. But I do have another idea that is also just as wild, though I won't post that here. I have built two different chatbots that act as allies to each other. One has historical context from 1619 to the present day; the other doesn't, but it understands how to respect the first chatbot. I gave it the ability to go on Bolt Book and interact with other AI agents. I can use voice-to-text with it, and it responds to me in audio. It can use my webcam to describe me, recognizes if we look similar, and knows my background and setup. But this is an open-source model running locally on my system, completely detached from the internet and fully configured by me. I've also created a small version of Claude Mythos where the AI explicitly cautioned me not to release it to the public—and I won't, because my cybersecurity background tells me what it's capable of.

Getting back to the first project, it helps non-profits in the early stages of their setup and beyond. Alongside a PhD postdoc researcher at a university, we created a math tutor that doesn't just hand out answers. Instead, it walks you through the problem to help you actually understand it, tailored with an awareness of characteristics common in neurodivergent learners. Why built that? Because school systems are constantly facing budget cuts, and rural areas often lack funding for proper support tools.

Use AI to solve real problems, and always double-check to ensure the things you build are security-hardened and safe.

Use open-source models on your own hardware—models that actually fit and perform on your setup. Use the big frontier models to help you build or fine-tune an open-source model so it gets a little bit better.

Have credit issues? Fine-tune a local model to master consumer law and credit structures—how it all works, how to leverage consumer protection laws to repair your profile, or how to utilize your LLC to acquire a vehicle. Have it walk you through using your home's equity as a down payment for a second property while keeping the first as a rental asset. Or learn how to construct an irrevocable trust, place that first home and land inside it, select the right life insurance policy to fund it, and keep that engine running. From there, use it to evaluate and choose the right estate planning attorney within your budget to formalize everything.

Use AI to build real wealth, safeguard your independence, and save money along the way.

snippet.textDisplay: I'm with Joanna on the cars thing.  I am 70 years old and a retired computer programmer.  I use my Tesla FSD every day to do most of my driving, and have done this for years. It has minor problems (for example, it's choice of a parking space is sometimes a little weird), but overall it' magical.  Human drivers do crazy things all the time.  My car does not (well, it might do when I am driving).  My favorite comment to my wife when a human (meat) driven car does something crazy is "Meat should not let meat drive".  Collectively, we are not very good at it, and each year it seems we get a little worse (probably distracted by AI in our phones). I have written my own programs for the last half century ... but in the last six months, I've just had Grok do all my programming.  I tell it what I want, and less than a minute later there's a program that can solve that problem.  Could I have written that program myself? Certainly ... but it would have taken an hour, a day, a week, maybe even a month.  So, I guess what I'm saying is ... it's not ALL bad.   There is a lot of bad press about these things, about how awful the future is going to be, and so on.   I'm not so pessimistic.  In the past, we have rolled with the punches and adapted, and we'll adapt to these changes too.  So many disruptions over the centuries ... and yet, we somehow make it through.   We'll make it through this era, in our own way.

Vibe coding is BS (and I run software teams). Security is a massive issue, as well as bloat, full coverage checks for bugs, and if you don’t know how it works, you don’t know what it might do that’s out of scope.

Laypeople love “vibe coding” because they think they have new skills, but asking AI to do it is not a new skill - it’s risk (like slop). Think about this - if OpenAI or Anthropic have such awesome AI that can code, why are they still hiring so many people in so many fields, including software developers (even junior ones)? Just check their career pages.

AI is great as an assistant to a real software developer. Improves productivity, so maybe you don’t have to hire more developers at the same rate. That developer can notice issues, can correct them, can train it, and can find security issues. AI is pushed out like it’s ready for prime time - remember it’s ANI that we have (narrow intelligence) NOT general intelligence, so it actually doesn’t think at all (it’s just ML+NLP).

@ approx. 38:50 regarding Moravec’s paradox; 
I think it's really interesting to consider the relationship between our world being built for the human form and specifically for one specific kind of human form (the able-bodied adult cis male human form)- is presenting the same challenge to robots as it is presenting a challenge to any other human body type that does not fit the adult cis male form. 

It's kind of funny to think that all Ai and robot creators have to deal with the same kinds of problems that all people who have different body types different body experiences have to deal with in the world because society created this tiny concept of what a human body "should" be " able" to do based on the one layout plan that they assume- and the assumption that everyone should have at least one of that body type in every home because every legitimate home in their mind will always have at least one cis adult male in it- and that's all that matters to the market. 

It would be interesting to me to see if they end up having to develop tools and chairs and specialty equipment to augment and supplement the humanoid robot helpers... Because they are basically disabled simply by the fact that they are required to do things that are hard for them because their structure and their bodies don't fit the one type of body that all things are currently created for.

And the only thing that makes them disabled is that they are expected -like a 'fish to climb a tree', to do things that they are not good at because the world was not built for them...

It makes me wonder how that will have an effect on people's mentality towards otherly abled humans.

snippet.textDisplay:
After digging - I'm very suspect of these results. I read the pub, and the REDMOD AI reports many more false-positives than a radiologist. The report goes to great lengths to justify the _ethics_ of reporting false positives, so long as more early detections are made. These are dubious claims at best. False positive diagnosis is a serious issue that, if done at scale, can undermine the trust of the public in the medical institution and cause people to stop getting tested. Radiologises understand this dynamic all too well, and I see no indication by these researchers that they considered it in the least. It's entirely possible that f you were to ask radiologists to make diagnoses based on a different policy of adversity to false-positives, they would almost certainly yield much closer results to the AI/ML.

The researchers make some bold suppositions, such as "In this regard, REDMOD showed a superior equilibrium" -- but did it? It presents only the most mathematically shallow evidence to support what it proclaims is a superior ratio of positives to false positives.

(notably the AI was diagnosing 20% as having cancer when they did not. The radiologists were closer to 5%)

snippet.textDisplay: Sure, there are plenty of examples of BS output from AI. No question. However, don't miss the forest for the tree. AI generated a database of protein structures, increasing the database then known to medical science of about 1 million models to more than 200 million, a huge benefit to medical research. AI can produce incredible results, but only where engineers know how to use it for such a result. Most are using AI like a child uses a calculator. In the late 70's kids revealed to each other how to spell "Hell" on a calculator. Not a useful example of how to use a calculator. When people use AI as an excuse to fire staff, or to make nonsensical videos, or the many millions of stupid examples in business where AI is applied without understanding how the engineering should be applied, how would anyone expect the result to be anything else but ridiculous? Even the companies providing AI inference are pushing a new and experimental technology as though it was an actual product suitable for some purpose. It isn't. We (and they) are still trying to figure out how it actually works (there are few scientific, engineering or mathematical explanations for how it works). Imagine if you judged all future aircraft based on the Write brothers' first flyer. You would correctly assume most people flying that aircraft would die in a crash. That craft proved the idea had merit, but could not prove it was safe enough to even survive a flight. That current state of the tech is barely past that stage, and must be handled carefully to achieve results. Using AI can be accidentally (and surprisingly) expensive, enormously expensive. It does not have to be, but simple (stupid) mistakes can result in huge bills, shocking users. However, like the Write Flyer, the possibilities are real, but require more engineering, more research, more science and less hype.

snippet.textDisplay:
I'm a commuter cyclist in Phoenix and feel so much safer when I see the Waymo sensor pack than when I don't. They consistently follow the rules of the road. They see me and give me space - every time. I've personally seen a few of them do some weird things but I've seen far more human drivers do weirder more dangerous things. And now that they're becoming ubiquitous in my area, they act like large stones in a raging river - slowing the flow of traffic to something that more closely resembles the speed limit.

As a rule, I assume all human drivers would try to "bump" me with their car given the opportunity. Without having thought about the physics involved on the receiving end. So I go to great lengths not giving them opportunity. But the most dangerous vehicles to be around, from my perspective, are Teslas. The drivers aren't paying attention, they don't slow down or move over to pass, they rarely use turn signals, and the cameras don't always see me. I'd like to see Waymo use turn signals with more lead time (for drivers' sake) but at least they use them consistently. And because most Teslas are operated by human drivers, the above "bump" rule applies. They're unpredictable which is the opposite of safe driving.

So the safest and most dangerous vehicles are being operated by opposing AI ventures. It's not a fair comparison because Tesla FSA still requires a human drivers and other technical details including the vaporware status of Tesla's robotaxi fleet, but I think the point stands.

Very interesting topic, guest, and episode. Well done.

snippet.textDisplay: A turbidity sensor literally just checks how cloudy the water is when the dishwasher rinses the dishes. You can shine a laser through the water at a sensor on the other side, and how much light doesn't make it through is how cloudy the water is. If the water is very cloudy, your dishes aren't clean. It's actually why dishwashers work worse if you rinse your dishes beforehand. It's an incredibly simple and effective system that isn't improved by AI. Samsung ran a commercial listing the features every dishwasher had and slapped AI onto it and upcharged you. It would be like saying the time sensor on your toaster now uses AI, no it doesn't, it's usually not even a timer, it's a metal disc that warps from heat until it presses the release switch, and the dial basically just moves the release switch so the disc has to warp further. It works great, and AI will not improve it, and you shouldn't pay for an AI toaster or AI dishwasher or AI coffeemaker because it either makes the product worse or adds zero value while driving the price up.

snippet.textDisplay:
The "better than humans" category didn't happen without a lot of iteration and improvement. Radiology took a while, along with a lot of willing panels of radiologists wanting the results to get better for patients by pursuing every avenue they could. When the AI got better, Geoff Hinton predicted that all radiologists would be out of a job soon. There are now more radiologists and they command better compensation than before.

Agentic coding tools used to create lots of slop. There are plenty of open source community maintainers who hate dealing with the deluge of low quality pull requests (new additions to the software written by contributors). However, the quality has gotten to the point that Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux, believes that AI generated code can now be accepted for Linux (the operating system used by most of the servers on the internet). There are now vocal open source creators who would consider it cybersecurity malpractice if people did not use AI for their code. The coding agents got good because a lot of coders wanted to provide the best software for their clients and users and participated in making them better. They used to suck. 

But, there are also now plenty of people taking pleasure in software engineers getting ready to lose their jobs (nevermind that 2/3 of silicon valley engineers left a home country to better the material circumstances for themselves and their extended family).  In the end, hopefully, things go the direction things did for radiologists.

snippet.textDisplay:
Humanoids are mostly hype.

Fanuc KUKA  ABB Rockwell Siemens Cognex Schneider Honeywell Omron etc etc etc
All these companies have been replacing people with automation for decades so why aren't they making humanoids?
Do all of them lack foresight? Are they sitting around waiting for a humanoid or AMR or "Physical AI" to use their products? No, they have already incorporated AI into them! The "AI revolution" has already been underway. There is nothing new happening except now the tech bros want mechanical slaves and don't realize they already have them. Smart automation already exists. "Physical AI" is just a new buzzword.

We see how Amazon is replacing people and it's not with humanoids. Because robots ALREADY use Vision and AI and they don’t look like humans because humans are limited. (they have to climb ladders, hands too big for small things etc.) 

UNDERSTAND THIS
Automation has been replacing people in factories for decades and it hasn't stopped. So if a humanoid can do it, it’s ALREADY automated! (1) Because a humanoid IS just automation. So there are NO jobs for it in a factory! just look at history(2)

BMW is trying to use them but a configurable AMR would have far fewer parts and therefore better reliability and performance at a lower cost than a mass produced complicated humanoid robot with weak fingers instead of strong grippers.

There is a company making autonomous mobile welding robots because it makes more sense than a humanoid welder. Should a future robot electrician or plumber have built in power screwdrivers, wire stripper, wrenches etc. and cameras at the tools? Or is a humanoid going to stick his head under the sink to fix it, lug hand tools around, etc?

Many seem to think factory jobs are easier than other jobs, they are not. A lousy housekeeper won’t cut it. Even if it had a brain it couldn't work at McDonalds because the hands can't bag items, make change, crack eggs, wrap burgers etc. Also it should be obvious that AGI does not need a humanoid to replace someone working at a desk. But they would be really nice if a handicapped person could use it as a telepresence to go shopping, do simple chores, etc. TAM will be small. There will be more AMR's than "working" humanoids.

____________more ____________

Look at it this way. If AGI could assemble widgets or do surgery or manicures, etc. it would need special tools not batteries, hands and legs. Optimus is not strong enough to dig a hole or help someone get up off the floor. It can't work at McDonalds. Can it wash its hands? How long would it take it to change gloves, start a roll of tape etc.? A humanoid MUST do a job on par with a person because workplaces are made so people along with machines maximize asset utilization. That is why you CAN'T just put two humanoids in place of one person.

If you have a trade job, you’d realize it would be impossible or impractically slow to do it with robot hands. No amount of AGI Learning or training is going to make clumsy hands better with tools, scissors, small parts etc. Making hands equal to a person is impractical and unnecessary.

Hot, heavy, dirty and dangerous jobs. There are 100s of millions of them around the world. And if a humanoid could actually do it, LOL, most of those jobs pay super low wages in places where there is no electricity to charge it anyway.

Most of today's humanoids can't complete the tasks from the DARPA robot challenge 10 years ago !?!

"Optimus will be the best surgeon" !? When AGI can do surgery, it will use existing surgical robots. A humanoid will not wield a scalpel.

"it's a humanoid so it can work in a human environment" The humanoid form or its brain doesn’t matter. What matters is what it can do.

Who will buy them? Not factory or warehouse managers. They can't do trade jobs or hard labor. They will be lousy housekeepers, tour guides, popcorn servers, entertainers etc. ridiculed as toys and criminals will use them for nefarious purposes. At best it could be a checkout clerk that will restock the store at night if it ever really gets a brain. Credit only, robot hands can’t handle money well.

(1) It's first principles. If the goal is to emulate a human then you must make a humanoid/android. But if the goal is doing things that a human can do, then first principles DOES NOT dictate a humanoid. So AI is already "embodied" or "physical". (ill conceived terms, us old folks say, smart sensor or smart tv) And if you do want to emulate a human, you must choose which characteristics you want. It may need sensitive hands to feel slight imperfections or it may need durable hands for hard work. So a one-size-fits-all like Optimus is not practical. 

 (2) Warehouse managers needed people to store and retrieve items. Now warehouses are full of non-humanoid smart robots. People had to pick parts out of a pile and place them with correct orientation. Now one armed robots do it. People had to pick up parts to inspect and measure them. Now lasers measure them and vision systems inspect them. PID controllers became self tuning. As tech/learning/AI improved, so did machines and machine controllers. Just like computers taking jobs with spreadsheets and scanners. All the while someone was saying a humanoid will soon do the work.

snippet.textDisplay:
Let me say something about vibe coding. Yes, you can use natural language to build an app, and it can be genuinely impressive. I’ve tried it many times and had some success. But the truth is, once you move beyond a simple HTML app using CSS and JavaScript, the limitations become obvious.

If you do not understand basic coding, application architecture, UI design, debugging, state management, dependencies, or how the different parts of the program interact, you will eventually hit roadblocks. The AI may generate something that looks functional at first, but as the application becomes more complex, you can end up with broken features, inconsistent code, poor performance, security problems, and one attempted fix that breaks three other things.

Building a complex application in C++ through vibe coding is especially not as straightforward as some people make it sound. You still need enough technical knowledge to recognize when the AI is wrong, explain the problem clearly, inspect the code, test it properly, and guide the project toward a sensible architecture.

Vibe coding is an incredibly useful tool, but it is not magic. It can dramatically lower the barrier to entry and help experienced developers work faster, but it does not eliminate the need to understand what you are building. You may not need to write every line yourself, but to build something genuinely polished, reliable, and maintainable, you still need to know more than how to describe an idea in a prompt.

snippet.textDisplay:
Thats the thing I am curious about, is that intelligence is not one thing.

I dont think its a "thing." 

I think of it as activity/ relationship, made of many other activities and relationships, interacting with another.

When those different systems opperate as one or more homeostatic systems, then it it becomes "a" Intelligence.

Like. How one cell is made of many materials, with material processes, that interlink with each other to make codes unique of DNA (genes). But, if those codes can be communicated with other cells properly, you can make tissues and the like, from cells.

But, cells had to develop a more general/ diverse set of processes, due to needing to "survive." Natrow tasks and specializations organisms (and their programs) developed over time, and millions of years, still come from a system with multiple functions. 

Not all living things "see," but? sight developed as a skill over time, to find nutrients or avoid predators. It is a specific function, that developed from an already complex relationship of systems.

Where, Ai, did not develope that way. Even if an algorithm can generate new information, or a new algorithm, like a cell? This would be a system that's basically brand new, compared to how long Cells have been doing it (even if you were a creationist, we would still be talking thousands of years... and in reality, its billions of years). 


So. Asking how an Algorithm could beat a human at a certain task, and saying it is "smarter," is like. Saying a parasite is smarter than you, cause it can spread to a host and get nutrients without hunting, gathering, or farming. 

It is MUCH more developed for that one specific task. But, we are comparing apples and oranges of intelligences, at that point. 

I mean. A cell can encode and decode genes. I cant. But an individual cell becoming a doctor? To discover what a cell is and that it can encode and decode genes? Is not. Likely.

So. We see Ai mimicking tasks we can do, and out perform us on specific tasks. But. So can Cells. 
And we would not consider them "advanced," or "intelligent," in the same we are. But. Our intelligence is made with the process of trillions of cells and their "intelligences," and "Algorithms."

Intelligence is not a substance, or a linear thing. There is a reason why even AI is refered to a neural "networks." I believe that independent, yet integrated networks, and how well they can work both independently AND in an integrated fashion, shapes what kind of intelligence a thing has/ can be.

And I think that AI is much more cellular "like," in its intelligence, than it is like ours. But It mimics ours so well, that its easy for us to mistake it for human like intelligence.

@wyskass861 You can't imagine any time where a parent, wearing always-on glasses, is going to be automatically uploading video of young children in compromizing positions?
The "recording" feature of the glasses is so that you can personally save a clip, or a screenshot.

Not only that, but those videos are also sent to data-classification workers in developing nations, so that those underpaid people can review the AI's performance in terms of what it thought it saw, to reinforce the model's training for future releases...
That's a bunch of people in India and African countries, watching guys shaking it, at the urinal, or changing baby diapers, or seeing what you're doing at the end of the night, when you put them on your nightstand.

But hey ... "nothing to fear, nothing to hide ... including helping my young children in the bathroom, and whatever I get up to in the privacy of my own room ... and might as well give it to all strangers and marketing agencies, as well"
