Things humans can't do (translating dozens of languages instantaneously during a conversation, for example) are a place where I can see technology connecting and strengthening humanity. I think there are still flaws there that we have to be realistic about, but I see potential.

It's the robot servant that you have to spend money on but doesn't get paid that gives me pause.

snippet.textDisplay:
@bulletsandbracelets4140 I think you missed the core point of the comparison. Nobody is claiming the computer or robot has feelings or is being "hurt." That's why my original comment was saying it goes back to psychology—the comparison is about human behavioral patterns and emotional dysregulation, not anthropomorphizing technology.

Psychologists directly study the link between venting rage on inanimate objects and subsequent aggression toward living beings:

Research on "Venting": A landmark study by Brad Bushman (2002, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 28(6), 724–731) demonstrated that venting anger on inanimate objects (like punching bags or smashing property) doesn't "release" anger—it increases physiological arousal and primes aggressive thoughts, making people more likely to act aggressively toward humans immediately afterward.

Clinical Standards: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) groups the physical destruction of property and physical assaults on animals/people together under impulse-control outbursts (such as in Intermittent Explosive Disorder).

Obviously, yelling at a frozen laptop doesn't automatically mean someone will assault a person. But psychologists treat object destruction and living-being aggression as shared behavioral indicators of poor impulse control.

Pointing out that aggressive behavior toward inanimate objects reflects on the person's emotional state isn't "treating an AI like a pet"—it's basic psychological science regarding human behavior.

snippet.textDisplay: As a doctor, AI has really made my work more efficient and I think its a win-win for doctors and patients. I’ve been using an AI scribe for about a year now, this means I enter the patients room with my phone in my pocket and start the visit (always getting the patients consent beforehand). I am able to focus 100% on the patient without having to write anything down and by the time I finish the visit and get back to my desk, the note is already done and ready on my desktop. For an AI note to be any good, you need to be very descriptive when talking to the patients so that AI captures as much as possible, so patients are happier because things are being explained to them in more detail. This has saved me hundreds of hours of note writing, about 10-15 minutes per patient. It has really been a gam changer for me and I’ve heard the exact same thing from many of my colleagues.

snippet.textDisplay: It's important to note that text transcription was around before GenAI was. What's important is to pay attention to what processing it does. What does it highlight in the summary and what does it dismiss? Statistical models already cause issues in medicine because certain things are overlooked due to rarity of disease, lack of data on certain sexes/races/income-levels, and popular recommendations. When we start trusting it implicitly to summarize properly without analyzing the results holistically, that is when it gets dangerous. I'm fine with a doctor recording our interaction, I'm not fine with a black box using that transcript to potentially influence my medical outcomes or history.

@tokashi1 I’ve worked with Amazon booksellers all my adult life and I never came across a “1 of 1” book. If it’s been published (as in typed and bound by a press in a publishing house), then there were more than 1 copies. But the issue is not whether you yourself would have had access to a rare book. You are 1 in 8.3 billion people living today. The problem is that when you destroy a book, it becomes unavailable to all 8.3 billion people living today and all the trillions and trillions of people that will exist after we’re long gone. It also means that anyone who ever wants access to that book will have no choice but to buy the AI.  
You might not think this is a huge problem. Well, I can tell you that booksellers are seeing massive sales right now, tens to hundreds of times greater than normal, and even though they know that the books are destroyed and once they’re gone they’ll be out of a business, they don’t care and they keep selling AI feeders the books. I can also tell you that some old and rare books have a lot of sentimental value. People ask for them on their death beds. People scour the internet to find that one title that helped them in childhood. Some collect signatures, rare editions, manuscripts, etc. People are willing to travel and spend a fortune to find a single copy of something they treasured and lost years prior. Well, when that’s all gone, books will become worthless. And as AI doesn’t just copy, but gaslight and manipulate information and brainwash its own user, the original point of reference will have disappeared and machines will control the narrative. You will no longer be able to check the verity of what you’re reading and learning. Your whole sense of reality will have been affected from the moment you learn to read; and you won’t learn to read from a book- you’ll learn to read from a screen.

snippet.textDisplay:
@pi3830 Honestly, I think this can have a lot of value. I'm single. Most of my friends live in other states, are married, are also busy, have different interests/budgets or are hermits that don't want to get out a lot. I love going to the movies, concerts, traveling, going to festivals, etc. Which means, I end up going alone most of the time. 

And that's fine. But sometimes it's easier when you have someone with you. Having a robot that can hold my drink while I go to the bathroom or can take a picture of me next to a cool statue or can remember where my car was parked in a giant parking lot would be helpful. And since I'm a woman, going out alone, often at night, they could add in safety features such as being able to protect their person from someone trying to rob or assault them. They could be programmed to notify emergency services in the event of a medical emergency. They could be programmed to be able to drive you home if you're intoxicated. 

If they had these features and were also programmed to be able to help around the house, it would be great. I live alone. It would be nice to have a robot to help me move my furniture if I want to rearrange my living room. Or help me with home improvements that normally require 2 people. 

I'm very happy being single and I never want to live with anyone. But sometimes I need help doing something and for whatever reason, the people in my life can't be there right that second to help. Having a robot around the house that CAN help would be very useful. You can have plenty of people in your life, but most people aren't around 24/7. Not everyone can drop what they're doing to help you turn a valve that you don't have the strength to turn on your own or cut down a limb from a tree that was struck by lighting and is dangling over your car.

snippet.textDisplay:
​​@lordbaphie I'm not sure why you're assuming that I'm privileged, considering that I belong to a middle-class family within a minority community. Yes, disadvantaged groups are more likely to face these risks, and it's important to take that into consideration. But this doesn't mean that people have to acquiesce to their current circumstances. Perseverance in the face of adversity can open up new avenues towards success. 

I'm not blaming anyone who has failed to find a stable relationship due to specific issues, but relying on a robot for emotional connection is not the solution. There are countless ways through which one can seek company in other people's presence, and we should strive to uplift one another. If we succumb to the capitalistic forces which seek to divide us, then the system will never change. Loneliness will continue to increase as these exploitative practices become entrenched in our society.

No one is mocking the people who turn to these robots for the sake of happiness. Instead, I'm concerned about their mental well-being. I strongly condemn the companies which take advantage of vulnerable people in order to maximise their profits. Recognising this issue is the first step towards helping those individuals. We shouldn't tolerate disingenuous solutions to the mental health crisis which plagues humanity. 

Obviously, those who have fallen through the cracks of the system shouldn't face mockery or slander. Yes, society is extremely hierarchical and prevents some people from attaining basic needs. This is precisely why we shouldn't accept these robots as an alternative to genuine relationships, because it serves as an indication to the elites that the working class is willing to rely on these unthinking machines for emotional support. Solving systemic inequalities requires a societal overhaul, which needs the mobilisation of the entire working class. Obviously, no single individual can achieve that, and we can't judge individuals who have given up. However, we shouldn't permit the elites to continue their exploitation through further distortions of reality.

snippet.textDisplay:
As technology continues to advance, we must remain spiritually discerning and guard our hearts. Not everything that promises comfort or companionship is truly beneficial for our souls.

Machines and artificial intelligence may be marketed as solutions for loneliness or emotional pain, but they can never replace the relationships God designed us to have with Him and with one another. If we begin to rely on technology to fill the places in our hearts that only Christ can heal, we risk becoming more isolated instead of more connected.

God created us for community, for family, and for fruitful lives that reflect His love. The enemy delights in anything that pulls us away from genuine relationships, weakens our dependence on God, or distracts us from His purpose. Scripture reminds us, “Be sober minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” 1 Peter 5:8  

As believers, we should approach every new technology with wisdom and biblical discernment rather than fear. Jesus warned that in the last days deception would increase (Matthew 24:4–5), so we must continually test everything against God’s Word and remain anchored in the truth.

Our hope is not in technology, but in Christ. He alone satisfies the deepest needs of the human heart. Let us pursue authentic fellowship, cultivate healthy relationships, and remain fruitful in the calling God has given us, trusting Him above every invention of man.
